speechtext:
I should like to say a word on this bill. This is not the first occasion that we have had this particular measure before us, and it is not the first occasion on which I have expressed my views in regard to it. The minister and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) have gone into the details of the bill quite sufficiently; therefore it is not my intention to deal with that part of it.
I want to speak more particularly with regard to the principle of the bill. We as a party have always maintained that we would do everything within reason to see to it that the workingmen of this country enjoy the greatest possible security in the field of trade unions, and the highest possible standard of living which they can attain. We have taken the stand that the voluntary revocable check-off is something the unions should have. As I have indicated on other occasions, we in Alberta have taken the lead in this country. Therefore we are just following the pattern which we have set in that particular legislation.
I recognize immediately, Mr. Speaker, the importance of having this legislation in the form of an amendment to the act itself, because it has been the experience of almost everyone who has had anything to do with labour organizations that some workers who enjoy the benefits that have been derived from the efforts of unions will take no part in financing the obligations of those unions. That is wrong. Anybody engaged in industrial labour should pay his fair share of the expenses incurred in getting the advantages. We know that from an industrial and economic point of view our whole national economy is dependent upon the amount of money which the labouring people, the agriculturists and others have to spend. If they

have not the money to spend, then of course the whole economy of the country is wrecked.
We recognize that immediately, Mr. Speaker, but I must point out, as I did on another occasion, one of the great objections I have to this type of legislation. I should not say "to this type of legislation", but more properly to the abuses to which it may lead. It is true that there are branches of labour organizations in this country who subscribe to the aims and policies of a political organization. I am not going to beat about the bush. The C.C.L. do subscribe to the political views of the C.C.F., and they have made the C.C.F. their political action arm. They may think that is proper.
I have always supported labour organizations, and they have always had my sympathy. Generally speaking, the people across this country are sympathetic to labour's aims, and they see the advantages of having a proper industrial organization in Canada; but at the same time a great many people object strongly to the unions siding with any political party. I have said without hesitation on occasions in my own riding, in the Drumheller valley and in East Calgary when that was part of my riding, both highly industrialized sections, that I would not want the unions to come out and support our organization as a political unit.
It is wrong. Every individual member of a union should have the privilege of supporting any political party he desires to support.
When you find some unions subscribing from $100,000 to $200,000 for political purposes during election periods then it is a bit out of reason. Some people say the money is not from such sources. However, I would maintain that if unions have that much money to put up for political purposes they do not have to extract such large amounts from the membership in the form of dues and in other ways.
I wish to make it quite plain that I am in wholehearted sympathy with workingmen. I want to see the unions progress. I want to see them with very strong labour union representation, and I want to see the voluntary revocable check-off instituted in law. I believe it is a good thing. But I would say this to unions. I believe it is unfair to the membership of the union and it does not serve a good practical purpose for any union to sponsor any political party.
Having said that may I say again that I am going to support this measure.

That a select committee to be designated be appointed to consider such of the estimates as may be referred to it and to report from time to time its findings and recommendations to the house.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
At five o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was dealing in general with the expenditures of crown corporations and their immunity from serious examination by parliament. They finance through parliament, but their responsibility to account for the moneys they receive and the manner in which they dispose of them is, to all intents and purposes, above consideration by parliament. There is, in truth, a committee on broadcasting to examine the affairs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and a sessional committee on railways to consider the auditors' report on the Canadian National Railways, but the examination made is ineffective and largely perfunctory.
I had referred to the request for information regarding the Queen Elizabeth hotel in

Special Committee on Estimates the city of Montreal, a matter that is very much in the minds of the Canadian people. It seems difficult for those with even a modicum of business experience to understand why a fabulous sum of money should be expended on the construction of a hotel by a public corporation which, instead of operating the hotel after completion, turns it over under lease to another company. I prefer to call it a lease, although the minister referred to it as simply a contract for operation.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext: For management, I said.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Yes. I did not have the exact nomenclature in my mind, but to me it is a lease. It is a difficult thing for people to understand the reason for the change of front. Certainly the hotel could not have been in its original concept simply a building to turn over on a management lease or a contract to a company outside of Canada, or indeed to any company in Canada. When a request was made for the production of the documents one would have thought that the minister responsible to parliament would have shown alacrity in giving the information. The minister, however, relied on the defensive stand that it was not in the public interest, and that the course of not revealing such matters which had been followed in the past was being followed in this case.
I am not dealing in any way with the decision that was made by the house yesterday, but I simply point out this, sir. If, indeed, that is the general regulation affecting parliament, then all I can say is that parliament pays the piper for some of these crown corporations, but they are able to dance to whatever tune they feel like dancing to, regardless of the attitude of the piper. To carry it a little further, the refusal in the public interest to answer a question such as this is tantamount to drawing the blind of secrecy in order to exclude the searchlight of full disclosure to parliament.
However estimable a minister of the crown may be, human nature being what it is there would be considerable temptation for the minister to take this stand when questions might be politically embarrassing. After all, if that power rests in a minister of the crown there is no question that could be brought before the House of Commons upon which the minister, so long as his party stood with him, would not be able to deny information by the simple expedient of saying it was not in the public interest.
So far as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is concerned, two years ago they defied the Auditor General, who said their system of bookkeeping was wrong and did not properly reveal the position of their

affairs. They paid no attention to him. Last November he repeated his criticisms, and since then the broadcasting corporation has decided to pay attention to the recommendations that were made. If the Auditor General, who is the watchdog above all watchdogs over expenditures, may be defied by any emanation of the crown, then indeed his operations are restricted, especially if the experience of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is repeated in other departments.
Several years ago, I think it was in 1951, there was another example at the time the Ford hotel in Montreal was purchased. It was only upon examination by the Auditor General that" it was revealed the building had not been purchased by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It was purchased by the international service of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which service occupied only a small portion of the building while the remainder was rented to the corporation. It is that sort of thing that arouses the interest and the proper criticism of parliament. The Auditor General pointed out that it seemed strange to him that such an irregular course should be followed. In reality, in his eyes, it seemed to imply that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was being indirectly subsidized out of the money provided for the international service.
I mention these two examples simply for the purpose of indicating that if, under our present system, when a minister of the crown may say it is not in the public interest to answer questions dealing with these matters he is fortified by precedent, then it is time in the interests of the public in general and a proper examination of the vast expenditures being made by these crown corporations that such a rule should be changed. Such a rule may have had its place 50, 75 or 100 years ago, or even up to 25 years ago when the state was not in public business to the degree it is today. Such a rule, however, applied to the conditions of today can only operate to shackle parliament in investigating expenditures and controlling waste.
So far as the motion before the house is concerned, it is an experiment. I am not optimistic about its success; for the committee system being what it is, with the committees having an overwhelming majority of representatives of the government, there is no real incentive on the part of the majority in a committee to permit matters to be brought before it that may be injurious to the government and the party to which they belong.
Human nature being what it is, I am not saying the situation would be any different

under another government; but the fact remains that in endeavouring to apply, even in a modified form, the American committee system to the British system of constitutional government, there has never been any great success. Endeavours to make it successful have reduced the dangers of the present situation, but have not materially improved it.
In Great Britain, as the hon. member for Eglinton pointed out today, one of the committees has as chairman a member of the opposition. If that system were followed in any of the committees of this house it might bring about at least a degree of interest in the activities of committees, and there would be hope for greater success than has been the general experience in the operation of committees during the time I have been a member of this house.
I do not desire to dash the hopes expressed that the committee will achieve what other committees have not achieved. It is an experiment and I hope it will succeed, because it would provide an opportunity for examination that the committee of the whole cannot provide, in view of the numbers constituting that committee. I do hope it succeeds; but I believe first and foremost, before the committee is set up, when the house moves to go into committee of supply there should be no endeavour to stifle discussion, or to deny to the opposition the opportunity to consider policy and offer such criticisms as in the opinion of the opposition are necessary at this time.
I mention but one department the estimates of which are to be submitted to this committee, that of immigration and citizenship. Mr. Speaker, there is a department that deserves examination and criticism in the house before the committee is set up, and it is but one of several that could be mentioned. I do not single it out for special attention. But I do say that when the committee is set up unless an opportunity is given to make suggestions and criticisms, the examination cannot but be perfunctorily confined to the various items, and the criticism of policy which is so necessary will be denied.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, quite a bit has been said with regard to this motion before us, to the effect that the appointment of a committee on estimates will be an experiment. I think when an experiment is being undertaken all the evidence of previous experiments along that line should be carefully examined, and care should be taken to see that the benefit of earlier experience is made available to us so we will not repeat errors
Special Committee on Estimates that may have been made by other parliaments, or other houses of commons, in dealing with this problem.
There has been plenty of criticism of the method of procedure in committee of supply, not only here but in the house at Westminster. People have pointed out the defects in connection with that particular problem which parliament faces each year. Now that we have reached this stage, when a committee on estimates is about to be appointed, it is worth while for us to consider all aspects of the matter and continue to make suggestions to the Minister of Finance so that he might modify the proposals he has presented to us, or take into consideration some points he may have overlooked.
In the first instance, what is the purpose of a committee of supply? Some people have said, and we also read in the newspapers, that the committee of supply exists to pass estimates each year. Well, that is so; but in actual practice what occurs? In May's Parliamentary Practice, fifteenth edition, where he deals with the committee of supply as it operates at Westminster, he points out that in the eighties of the last century the opportunities for a general debate when the house went into committee of supply were limited to four occasions. He says that in 1947 this restriction was removed, and that 26 days are now permitted for consideration of supply. Then he adds this sentence at page 705 which, I suggest, is worthy of note:
It was intended that facilities for the criticism of departmental administration (now recognized as the real business of supply) should be available throughout the session, not merely during the period when there were estimates before the house.
It is not possible to underline sentences in Hansard, but the words to which I want to draw attention are those in brackets, "now recognized as the real business of supply"- namely the criticism of departmental administration.
That is a different concept from the prevailing opinion that in committee of supply our main business is to examine the figures placed before us, and to vote on them as we reach the end of the discussion of the estimates of a department. I realize there has been a considerable volume of criticism across the country with regard to committee of supply, and the statement is frequently made that at the last moment millions of dollars are voted without careful consideration. I am not at all sure that criticism is going to be met by the proposal now before us.
We have had our attention drawn to the work of the external affairs committee over the years. Those who have been on that
966	HOUSE OF
Special Committee on Estimates standing committee of the house have indicated to us that that is a good method of dealing with estimates. They have the advantage of experience on that committee, which I have not had; but for the last two years, though I have not taken the opportunity here in the house to express it, I have been objecting to that method of dealing with estimates in the committee on external affairs, for this reason. Those of us who are not on that committee never have the opportunity to examine the external affairs estimates here in the House of Commons. We have no opportunity of putting questions to the minister. That is all done in committee.
I am told "If you are not informed, read the reports of the committee on external affairs". We have so many reports of various committees to read that it is very difficult to keep abreast of what is going on, and some committee reports are not published very quickly. They do not appear, as Hansard does, the following morning. Therefore I have been suggesting that the external affairs estimates might very well be considered in the committee of the whole.
It might be said, "Well, you would not want to do that all the time". Perhaps not, but once in a while let them come forward here, let the whole house have a go at those estimates, let the whole house interrogate the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Why should he be relieved of questioning in the house on the ground that there has been an opportunity to debate external affairs on the first item and again when the report of that committee comes to the house? There would be no particular harm in subjecting the minister of that department to the same system of interrogation that other ministers have to experience in getting their estimates through the house, and we would all have an opportunity to learn some of the details of that department. That is a contrary point of view to that which has been presented up to date, but it happens to be my opinion.
It is on the basis of the experience of the external affairs committee that the proposal has been brought forward that other departments be examined in the same way. Several references have been made to the experience in the House of Commons at Westminster. I would like to add a little to those references and point out one or two things which seem to indicate that even there the committee on estimates has not been an unqualified success. I shall quote three or four short passages from that excellent standard work called "Parliament", of which the author is W. Ivor Jennings. On page 259 he says this:
The function of the committee of supply is to examine and consent to the estimates. In practice


it is impossible for a committee of 614 members to do anything of the kind. Indeed, it is impossible for a small committee to consider them with any degree of success, even if they are all prepared to study 1,500 pages of figures and explanations and to undertake the long preliminary study which is essential.
Then he deals with the actual work of the committee of supply in the house, and quotes various people who had long experience in the House of Commons at Westminster. On page 298 I find this:
The debate is technically a discussion on proposed expenditure. Its purpose is sometimes said to be to induce economy in the government; though, as Mr. Lloyd George has said, "it generally ends in a demand that you should spend more money for something or other".
There is a notation at the bottom of that page. He says:
Compare Mr. Gladstone's statement; "It is more difficult to save a shilling than to spend a million."
The problem was acute even as long ago as Mr. Gladstone's time. Further on Mr. Jennings goes on to say:
For all these reasons debates in supply are often criticized. Lord Eustace Percy once called them "the most discursive and futile of all our proceedings."
With that some of us here would be in agreement. I continue:
On the other hand, Sir Austen Chamberlain said: I think they (supply days) are admirable. With the additional occasional vote of censure, they give the private member of the opposition sufficient opportunities for discussing policy, and I do not believe that you can do more in the House of Commons. I do not think that in these days the House of Commons will ever control the details of expenditure. You have to rely for those upon the departments whose business it is to control them. The more opportunities you give to the House of Commons to discuss supply, the more pressure is put upon ministers to spend money.
Then on page 303 he deals with the actual work of the estimates committee, and points out that proposals to establish an estimates committee were made in the house at Westminster from 1880 on, and at various times committees were set up. Reports were brought in suggesting changes and alterations. They had considerable difficulty in determining just what the committee on estimates might do. On page 303 Mr. Jennings says this:
At no time since 1902 has it been suggested that the committee of supply has been an effective means of controlling expenditure, or even a body concerned primarily with expenditures.
Hence the necessity of having a committee on estimates to look after the detail, letting the committee of the whole house deal with questions of administration and policy. Then he considers the success or failure of the committee on estimates in that house over a period of years, and quotes from the comptroller and auditor general, who, in 1931, was

Sir Malcolm Ramsay. This is what the auditor general said at that time:
The estimates committee has, I am afraid, failed to realize the expectations of those who advocated its establishment. It is true that it has helped to secure certain useful improvements, generally of a minor order, but it has effected no substantial economies and its results have surely been achieved by disproportionate expenditure of time and labour by members and witnesses, and some at any rate of the matters on which it has made recommendations might equally well have been handled by the public accounts committee (e.g. the regrouping of the estimates, or the financial control of the empire marketing board).
The last quotation I shall read is simply this, and it is the opinion of Mr. Jennings after his lengthy examination of the work of the estimates committee in the British House of Commons. At page 312 he says:
The estimates committee is not completely useless. It was particularly useful in re-establishing and reinforcing treasury control after 1920. For the most part, however, it duplicates work done more effectively by the public accounts committee.
Then he goes on to show that the public accounts committee has advantages that the estimates committee does not enjoy. For one thing, the chairman of the public accounts committee is the choice of the opposition; for another, it has the auditor general and various people to assist, whereas the estimates committee has not that assistance granted to it.
The weaknesses of the present plan must be obvious after the speeches we have heard on this subject, and I hope the Minister of Finance will take careful note of the various suggestions that have been made. It is rather a mistake to think that we can effectively control the expenditures that come to us outlining government policy. Every item in the estimates is a government measure; it is not possible to have an item reduced except with the consent of the government, nor is it possible to have items voted down without the government being called upon to resign. Therefore everything that comes before us is actually a government measure presented to us, and it is difficult for us to deal with those estimates from the standpoint of people who are anxious to effect economy. Yet parliament gets the blame for passing enormous sums of money in a few moments at the close of the session, as though we were all to blame for what is going on.
Surely we of the opposition cannot be blamed for what is actually in effect government policy. Our course is to attempt to indicate to the government that their expenditure is wrong, that there should be economies effected, or that there has been waste and extravagance in certain fields. But we as an opposition cannot effect economies which are
Special Committee on Estimates in reality in the hands of the government. We can talk and vote against the government's declared policy, and they stand or fall by the acceptance or rejection of their policy.
The present proposal does not in my opinion hold out any great hope of a change in that situation. I would have been prepared to accept the proposal in a more cheerful spirit had the minister not hedged it around with certain restrictions. The restriction to which I object is the one to the effect-if I understood the minister correctly-that we would not be able to have a debate on the administration and general policy of a department if the estimates of that particular department were transferred to this committee on the estimates.

speechtext: You did.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
I am happy to have his correction. If we in the House of Commons can still have a debate on any of these departments before they are dealt with by the estimates committee, or after they return from that committee, then I believe that is a proper safeguard. However, I am not sure that is what the house gathered from the minister's earlier statements. I believe the minister said the committee on estimates was going to conduct its proceedings after the fashion-of the committee of the whole house, and that on the first item that committee would discuss administrative policy and subsequently ask the minister questions. If we in this house can retain the right and opportunity to criticize the minister's administration and the policy of the government, then that is a real safeguard, and under such circumstances I might be inclined to support this proposed experiment.
But we want to be fairly certain that this is going to be the case because, as others have already pointed out, it is here in this House of Commons that the effective work of parliament is done. There is a great deal of work done in committee, but committees do not have public opinion focused upon them as is the case in the house; and I for one would not be in favour of a great deal of the work of the house being done in committee. I know there are opportunities in some committees to make a more detailed analysis of various matters that come within the scope of investigation, and that officials and other people may come before such committees and give evidence. Nevertheless, the work of committees does not receive the same attention by' the press or the public as the
968	HOUSE OF
Special Committee on Estimates work that is done here in the house, and I would not care to release any minister from his duty to rise in the house in the glare of public opinion and state his case with regard to his department.
I shall conclude with this observation. I believe it would be a mistake-and again the minister may correct me if I misunderstood him-to have a committee of supply examining departmental estimates in this chamber and at the same time a committee on estimates examining some other department in some other part of this building. We would have the main House of Commons and a minor house of commons operating at one and the same time. It seems to me that would detract from one or the other and my preference is to retain the discussion here in the House of Commons.
If the minister is prepared to modify his proposal, outline the safeguards and make certain we have every opportunity of interrogating ministers on administrative policy, I would say he might go ahead with this experiment. But I hope no one is going to be carried away by the expectation that large economies will be effected or that the house is going to gain greater control over the expenditure of money by parliament. It must be emphasized that these are government measures under government control. That, Mr. Speaker, concludes my observations with regard to this particular matter.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I hope the minister and the house* are not feeling too impatient at this moment, because the minister himself referred to the fact that a motion was made in 1921 for the setting up of a committee on estimates. I have read the debates of that day and the marginal notations as to the time the debate occupied, and I would point out that the debate occupied two hours and 40 minutes, at the end of which the motion was withdrawn.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
The same thing might
happen today.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Therefore in 1921 they were discussing an entirely academic question. I might point out in addition that the time was mainly occupied by speakers sitting in opposition to the government. Tonight, however, we are discussing a proposal which is far from academic and which, if adopted, will become the pattern for the conduct of the discussion of this house for a good many years to come.
I say this is far more than an academic discussion because the motion was spoken to by the Minister of Finance on behalf of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), and it obviously carries all the considered opinion and weight of the government majority behind it.

It is perhaps odd to note that the time taken on this debate up to this moment is exactly two hours and 40 minutes, and I hope the minister will not become impatient if we wish to express our views on the proposal now before us. I feel that a proposal for an experiment such as this is one which we as interested commoners should be ready to support. I have been a member of the committee which with Your Honour has been considering possible revision of the rules of the house, and I have in a general way expressed support for a proposal of this sort in that committee.
I am not going to back away from that position, though I confess I was disturbed by the minister's approach to this problem of setting up this committee when he spoke this afternoon, because I do feel if I understood him correctly that his proposal falls considerably short of the sort of committee we had under consideration, and which we had considered adopting as an experiment.
In my approach to this whole problem I want to say at the outset-and I know I share the views of all other hon. members here-that I get a little bit tired sometimes when I hear people criticize members for taking time in parliament. Parliament is the place where we are supposed to talk about the affairs of the nation, and particularly it is the place where we are supposed to discuss the spending of the money of the people who make up this nation.
I believe in parliament as an institution where we should discuss intelligently the affairs of the nation but where, it is quite true, we should not waste our time or the time of others by discussing them unintelligently, that we should not use our time inefficiently. I agree with the other opinion that has been expressed-I think the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis) and others in my own party expressed it, and also the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power)-that the mere desire to cut down the time expended is not necessarily conducive to the more efficient conduct of the business of parliament.
I believe in parliament as an institution. I believe that parliament will work only as well as its members make it work. This proposed committee will therefore work only if its members-and they will be the same people who are members of the House of Commons-will make that committee work. They can make it work, in my submission, only if they approach their task in an attitude of mind in which they recognize that they are members of the House of Commons, and that their job is not to expedite the passing

of estimates but rather to examine closely whether or not the estimates are justified. If that committee approaches its work in the sense that it is a committee to get the estimates through more quickly I venture to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it will not be doing the work of the House of Commons, and that it will not be really in a true sense expediting the work of the House of Commons.
I am not an expert in this field. I have not been here very long. However, I have tried to do some reading and to absorb some feeling of what it is to be a member of the House of Commons and of what the House of Commons means. All my reading has convinced me that a member will not really advance the affairs of the nation as a member of parliament unless he as an individual is convinced of the importance of being a member of parliament; and being a member of parliament should mean the same on both sides of the house. If you go back to the old days in history you will find that the ordinary commoner, the member of parliament, was a person whose will and wishes were opposed to the will of the executive; and his job as a commoner was to seek to make certain that the will of the executive was not imposed upon the people contrary to the wishes of the people. It is in that sense that I feel we fall down in our approach to the task of being members of the House of Commons today.
I am not going into a lengthy criticism of the party system, but I am going to say this. I think that to too great an extent we are divided into members who support the government whether the government is right or not, and members who criticize the government whether the government is right or not. I believe what we should try to do is instil into members of this house a sense of being commoners, representatives of the people as opposed to the executive who are seeking-for motives of convenience, ease and expediency -to circumvent, if you like, the House of Commons.
It therefore seems to me that the job of the committee on estimates, whether it be the committee of the whole house, the committee of supply or the special committee now contemplated, should be to examine the estimates in a common spirit, not as members of the government trying to get them through more quickly or as members of the opposition trying to stop them from going through. It seems to me that we should examine the estimates as members of the House of Commons trying to see collectively whether the expenditures proposed by the government are justified and are in the best interests of the people.
Special Committee on Estimates
Unless this committee when constituted approaches its work in that spirit I believe it will not in fact expedite the work of the house or increase the prestige of the house, but rather will in fact make it more convenient for the government to get its estimates through with rather less trouble even than it had before.
I looked with some interest at the debate referred to by the minister in introducing this motion. There are some extremely interesting quotations in that debate. I start with the quotation by the hon. member who introduced the motion, namely Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux who read-and this I want to lay before the house for its consideration in setting up this committee-a passage from Bagehot on the English constitution, as follows. I am reading now from page 2193 of Hansard of 1921. He said this:
The House of Commons-now that it is the true sovereign and appoints the real executive-[DOT] has long since ceased to be the checking, sparing, economical body it once was. It now is more apt to spend money than the minister of the day. I have heard a very experienced financier say: "If you want to raise a certain cheer in the House of Commons, make a general panegyric on economy; if you want to invite a sure defeat, propose a particular saving."
That, of course, is the task which confronts all of us. It is the task with which we are all faced as members of the House of Commons. No one knows it better than the Minister of Finance, and there is no one who, when he stops to consider it, knows it better than the private member on the government side. As I see it, this is a collective task we have to do in setting up a committee that will approach its work in a spirit in which-perhaps because it operates with a little less publicity than does the committee of the whole house-they will say to themselves not "How will this look in my own riding?" or "How will this look in my own province?" but rather "We in the committee are all members of the House of Commons; we are all commoners, and here we have presented to us the proposals of the executive to spend the money of our people, the common people, the people we represent. Let us all go to work on them".
If we approach the matter with that attitude, remembering that even in the House of Commons it is perhaps more apt to invite defeat than to invite success to suggest a saving, because of the party lines that are drawn here, then perhaps in the committee that is to be set up we may be able to circumvent that tendency which I have outlined.
No House of Commons in the committee of the whole, or no special committee of the house, will work unless we have a sense of

Special Committee on Estimates our position as members of the house and a sense of our responsibilities as commoners in relation to the proposals placed before us by the executive. I think it is interesting that this proposal comes before us at this time, spoken to by the new Minister of Finance who has just recently taken over his portfolio. When I learned of his new appointment, Mr. Speaker, I wrote him a personal letter of congratulation and good wishes for success in his task. Therefore I can say what I have to say by way of public criticism in the knowledge that he has my good will as a fellow member of the house, and one who is entrusted with a very important portfolio of government in this country.
But I might then perhaps be permitted to express the hope that in introducing this motion to set up a committee he is not just looking for a whitewash, just seeking to constitute a body which will make it easier for him to get his estimates through, a body to which he can point and say, "Well, look; the estimates committee approved these things. What are you people doing criticizing them out on the platform?" I hope he is not trying to constitute a body which will be dominated by the government majority but that it will be, as I say, a body which will approach its task in the spirit I have tried, in a very imperfect way, to indicate I think it should be approached, namely in the spirit of commoners, of members of the House of Commons together.
Incidentally, I hope too that if the experiment should fall short of the hopes which we in the opposition, and I am sure members on the government side, have for it and, therefore, we are compelled on some later occasion to say that we do not like your estimates committee any more, the minister will not say, "But you approved the motion unanimously in the house." I admit, even while sounding these words of caution, that I am prepared to support the motion because I hope the experiment will work, but I am going to do as other members have done and suggest some positive changes in the approach to the committee differing from those which were suggested by the minister. Therefore I say again that I hope the minister is not just looking for ways, as it were, of making his extractions more painless. I hope the minister has not taken a course in painless dentistry.
I want to refer the minister to some other words uttered in the course of the debate to which he himself referred, as found at page 2201 of Hansard of April 18, 1921. It is true that the hon. gentleman, Mr. Michael Clark, then member for Red Deer, covered quite a

wide field and discussed various types of taxation which I know will be of interest to the Minister of Finance, but I think what he had to say is perhaps applicable tonight in the circumstances in which we find ourselves. He was discussing a motion to set up a committee on estimates, and said:
I venture to think that well as my hon. friend the minister of finance is shaping in his new office, at the present time he is looking anxiously for some method by which he may pluck the goose without making her squawk. Well, I trust he will not be too successful in his researches in that direction but will assume an attitude of stern public morality and seek out methods of taxation which will be righteous and just methods, and that he will not care whether the application of them is accompanied by considerable squawking on the part of the goose. As a matter of fact, it is only when you make the electors complain that you make them understand what your policy has cost them, in whatsoever line that policy may show its activities.
So I hope the minister, in introducing the motion to set up a committee, is not just seeking a more painless method of dealing with the estimates. I think the estimates should be a very painful subject of consideration in the House of Commons. I think we should make them a painful subject for the ministers who bring their estimates before us, because I think only in that way will we in fact be doing our collective duty as members of the House of Commons.
I should like to echo the words of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), trying not to adopt a tone of lecturing or moral rectitude, and suggest in all sincerity and in a spirit of comradeship to members on the opposite side that if they will join us in examining and cross-examining the government in the house and in the estimates committee not only will we welcome their help but they will find it a rewarding and, indeed, a rather enjoyable task. I hope they will approach the proposed committee on estimates in that spirit, and not try to make it easier for the ministers and the departmental experts who appear before the committee to get away with their proposals for expenditure.
I shall conclude in a few words by suggesting a different approach to the committee from that which I understood to be outlined by the Minister of Finance today. I do not consider that the committee on estimates should be modelled on the committee of supply. I think rather that the committee should concern itself with dollars and cents exclusively. I think the committee should have before it all the departmental officials who are responsible for the expenditure and administration of the items of the departments which come under the scrutiny of that committee. I think these experts should answer directly to the committee.

I believe it would be a great mistake to repeat in the committee on estimates the process we see here in the house where a member asks a question of the minister, the minister leans over the desk and listens to the departmental experts, quite often misunderstands them or fails to hear them because there is a buzz of conversation behind him or on this side, and then gives an answer. Then you see the deputy tugging the minister's sleeve, the minister leaning over again and then saying, "I am sorry, I misunderstood my hon. friend's question", when in fact he has misunderstood his deputy's answer, and corrects himself in what he has just said.
I quite agree that on the floor of the house-it can only happen when we are in committee-the minister must answer. Civil servants cannot speak here, and that procedure is proper even though cumbersome. But if we are going to set up a committee on estimates it will negate the whole purpose of the committee if we have to go through that procedure. I think the committee must have the right to question departmental officials directly, because they are the ones who are going to spend the money.
Also, approaching it in the spirit that the committee will work within the confines of government policy, I think we should be entitled to say to the deputy minister or associate deputy or head of a branch: This government policy says you shall have so many offices, let us say, where immigrants will be admitted, and you are admitting so many immigrants a year. Why do you need X thousand dollars to do it? How do you propose to spend those thousands or hundreds of thousands of dollars?
That is the sort of work with which the committee should be concerned, and it is the sort of questioning which I do not think should be conducted through the indirect channel of a question to the minister, back to the deputy, back to the minister and then back to the member asking the question. It would take too much time in the first place, and I do not think you get sufficiently direct answers or a sufficiently complete process of examination and cross-examination.
That being the approach I should like to see followed, without laying down a blueprint I think a measure of consultation with the opposition should be recognized as to which departments should be referred to the committee. I know the government has to exercise responsibility and I am not seeking to deprive it of that responsibility because I expect, hope and intend to hold it responsible for all its acts; but when it comes to this business of the House of Commons examining the activities of the government 50433-62J
Special Committee on Estimates I think there should be a measure of consultation between the government and the opposition as to which departments it will be most appropriate in the public interest to place before the estimates committee. The government of course, I admit, would have to reserve, as it always must do, its right of final decision, if you like. I am only asking for a pattern to be established, that we should not be confronted at the outset with a decision that these are the departments that are going to go before the committee. Let us have at least a measure of consultation before that decision is made.
In that light I make this suggestion. The one department which this year should not go to the committee on estimates is the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. There are several departments, I feel, on which a discussion of policy is required. I see the minister smiling. I am not going to read anything into his smile. I was going to say this even before he smiled. I believe he will agree with me that it has been several years since we have had a real opportunity to discuss the policy of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration in committee of supply.
Taking the approach I do that a committee on estimates should be a committee on dollars and cents and not on policy, I feel that one of the departments which should not at this time be referred to the committee on estimates is the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. I would hate to see an attempt made to discuss policy in the house here and have the government say we should not discuss policy on the motion to refer the estimates, we should wait until the estimates come back from the committee on estimates. Then in the committee on estimates they would say, "This is not a suitable place for a discussion of policy; wait until this committee reports to the committee of supply." The report of the committee of supply is made on the last day of the session, and we would be placed in the same situation in which we were placed by the minister last year, when we had about seven and one-half hours on the last day of the session to discuss the policy of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
These are the main suggestions I have to make with regard to this committee. Before the government lays before us a final decision as to how this committee should operate I believe there must be a good deal more discussion in the committee on rules, which is now meeting with Your Honour, as to the pattern which should be followed; as to whether that committee should be a dollars and cents committee, a mixed dollars and cents and policy committee or a policy committee; whether we should have a discussion

Special Committee on Estimates on policy when the motion is made to refer the estimates of the department, or whether that discussion should take place when the estimates committee reports back to the house. The last thing I want to see is a discussion of policy thwarted because the estimates of the department are being referred to the committee, then have the estimates committee report back to the house on the last day of the session and have us find we are deprived of the right to discuss policy.
These are the dangers. I admit I am drawing attention to the dangers. I am doing so because I approach this subject in the spirit that the government has asked us to embark on an experiment. I am prepared to embark on the experiment, but I am not prepared to support that experiment for one day longer if I become convinced this is becoming, intentionally or otherwise, one more tactic for making it easier for the government to impose its will on the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext: If the minister speaks now, he will close the debate.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext: When I was considerably younger than I am now, Mr. Speaker, I heard Admiral Beatty refer to the agreement between the United Kingdom and the United States to settle the war debt, and his remark was that if it cost so much to win a war, what would it cost to lose one? I have been reminded of that today because I thought I was introducing a motion which had been requested on innumerable occasions in this house by the opposition. I wondered, in fact, if my senses had left me, and if I had not heard the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) on many occasions in the past six or seven years say that if only we had an estimates committee we would save a lot of time in this house; we would have a better discussion, and the constitution would be saved rather than ruined as some hon. members across the way would indicate now.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext: You made it too conditional.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Yes, 1 suppose we have to have conditions in the House of Commons; we have to lay down rules to carry out the business of the house. I am particularly glad that I did lay down some rules with respect to this committee in my opening remarks, because it is quite evident that if I had not the opposition would not be able to agree on a single thing the committee ought to do when it meets.
Just to be very brief about it, the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) indicated that his group would support this measure


and asked one specific question which I should answer. He requested that there might be a change in the personnel of the committee from time to time because the opposition, and presumably the government side, would be desirous of taking care of those who had an interest in one department and not in another. I do not believe the government has ever refused to change the name of anyone on a committee if a party desired to have a change made, and that will continue to be the case. I would hope that in this way we would have the best possible experience brought to bear on the estimates from time to time in the estimates committee.
The hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) said he approved of the proposal, and wanted it made clear that there would be an opportunity in the committee to hear from officials of the departments for the purpose of eliciting information. He rather indicated that he thought the only way to do that would be to have the officials there, and not have an examination of the minister intervening. Now, I have not the blue sheets of what I said, but at that point I read very carefully the notes I have in front of me and I am going to reread the point I made, and which he must have overlooked in his remarks. I said this:
Each minister would be responsible for the conduct of the affairs of his department before the committee, and if he chooses to make all the answers himself, that would be consistent in our view with the purposes of the committee. If, on the other hand, he thinks it desirable to leave the explanation of the details of administration to others, that will also be his responsibility, but if this course is followed it will not be possible for an official or other person to be questioned as to the policy of the government. This must be the responsibility of the government and the minister concerned, and he cannot devolve that responsibility upon an official.
I take that to mean, Mr. Speaker, that in all probability ministers will prefer to have officials, from time to time, speak directly to the committee. But I repeat that is a matter of choice for the minister as to how he conducts his affairs before that committee. I cannot conceive of that committee having any greater authority than the committee of supply. I tried to make that point throughout everything I said.
The hon. member for Eglinton raised a number of questions, and in particular he seems to have taken objection to the thought that there would not be a debate on policy on the motion to send these estimates to the estimates committee. He pointed out that there had been debates on policy with respect to external affairs when we sent the estimates of that department to the standing committee on external affairs. It is quite true that in recent years we have followed

that course, particularly because there has been some anxiety in the house about external affairs matters during the last four or five years.
I should like to point out that it is only a practice which has grown up. We did not always follow it. In the first three years, 1946, 1947 and 1948, there was no debate on the motion to refer the estimates to the standing committee, and in 1952 there was no debate. Of the six or seven times we have followed this practice, there has been just about an even division as between debate or no debate.
The government has always acceded to the request of the opposition for a debate on external affairs. On occasion we have resorted to the device of moving the adjournment of the house to permit that debate. In my view that system, that practice, can be followed on any future occasion when there is an obvious need for debate on external affairs. But the point I wished to make-and I am sure the point was made clearly, though I understand I did not make myself clear to the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill)-was this, that if there is any advantage whatever in a discussion of these estimates in a room other than this one, surely the opposition would not expect the government to follow their wishes in that respect and, in so doing, take more time in this room in a debate on policy.
Now, I said that a motion to refer these estimates to the estimates committee should not be debatable. That was all I said. I did not say-and I am sure no one else understood me to say-that that would preclude debate in the committee of supply itself. I think it is perfectly obvious from the remarks of the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) why I went no further than that.
There has been a great deal of discussion as to when you can have a policy debate to the best advantage. One argument which has been advanced on innumerable occasions by the Leader of the Opposition was that if we only had an intimate, detailed discussion of the estimates first, we could have a better debate on policy afterward. So, as I conceive the practice here, we intend to send these estimates to the estimates committee. Hon. members will there be able to ask all the questions which they say they have not a chance to ask in committee of supply, or that they do not feel like asking because they appear to be trivial and they do not want to hold up the house. They can ask all these questions and get the information they want, then when the item comes back to committee of supply we will have, as we always intended
Special Committee on Estimates to have, a debate on item 1, such as we have always had; and that debate may very well be longer and more specific and better informed because of the preliminary discussions in the estimates committee.
That I thought was one of the most telling arguments in favour of this practice. Now we find that the opposition is hopelessly divided as to whether that ought to be done. The hon. member for Prince Albert for example wants to have the policy debate before these items go to the estimates committee. Well, if he has the debate before, I am sure he need not have one after. At any rate it is not the intention of the government to extend the time for consideration of the estimates.
The hon. member for Greenwood was less than enthusiastic about what we were proposing to do, as I understand him. In fact, if I were to judge his position-

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext: Hopeful.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext: -it would be that he had some genuine doubts as to the usefulness of the estimates committee or, alternatively, that he was afraid that ultimately this would lead to a diminution of the responsibilities of the committee of supply. If he did not think those things, there was no point in quoting Walter Elliot, who expressed great concern about the difference in the consideration of the estimates in the House of Commons at Westminster at the time he was speaking, and what it had been on former occasions. I would suppose that the hon. member for Greenwood does not share the view that this committee can add very much to the usefulness of the committee of supply. We all hope it will; we think it will. But I want to assure him, and I want to assure all hon. members- because I was surprised by the suspicions which appeared to be in their minds about our motives-that this motion is as a direct consequence of our repeated discussions on this subject of aiding in the consideration of the estimates, and in the work of the committee of supply.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext: Would the minister permit a question? Does he think it unnatural and unreasonable that on this side we should have thought, as I did, that the general pattern would be that which was followed with regard to external affairs? That was what I understood, and I would like to ask the minister if he thinks that was an unnatural and unreasonable understanding.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
The estimates of the Department of External Affairs have been referred to the standing committee since the immediate post-war years. At that time it was the intention and the hope-and I think in the
974	HOUSE OF
Special Committee on Estimates main the hope has been realized-that external affairs would remain an all-party consideration. That was the reason in the first instance it was possible to adopt the practice of sending those items on external affairs to the standing committee for further consideration. It was felt that external affairs, as a policy, was something that all parties ought to be involved in to the greatest possible extent, and that that in itself would lead to the committee extending its influence over matters of external affairs. But it was not considered at that time that a reference of the items to the standing committee would have any particular influence over the actions of the committee of supply. It was not requested that we should do what has been done for the purpose of simplifying debate in the House of Commons, in committee of supply, on external affairs estimates. It was for the purpose of a more general understanding of the policies of external affairs.
Now, over the course of two or three sessions, or perhaps three or four, one would suppose that he would get around to all the departments in the estimates committee. That is the intention, and I agree that hon. members opposite might find it convenient to consider a particular department next year or the year after which they would not want to have this year. I have no reason to suppose we shall not consult them about their convenience in this as we have in other matters.
However, as the hon. member for Kamloops indicated, we felt we were under an obligation to lay down a practice for this year by selecting the particular departments that have been mentioned. And just one word about that. We find the extraordinary situation of the hon. member for Prince Albert wanting to discuss the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, and wanting to discuss it before it goes to the estimates committee and when it comes back, and the hon. member for Kamloops saying that is the one department that should not go to that committee.
It would not be confessing anything that is not known to the house if I pointed out that I was responsible for the policy of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration until recently. I am not unaware of the fact that the opposition, through the leader of that party, has demanded a royal commission with respect to immigration. And this government has no intention of granting that request. On the other hand it did seem to us that by offering this department to the estimates committee for the kind of consideration they say they have not been able to give it in committee of supply, we were doing everything short of that in accommodating them.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext: It was just because of the lack of time in committee of supply. It was brought up on the last day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext: I am prepared to speak about that, too, if my hon. friend wishes. It was not the last day; it was the last two days my hon. friends debated citizenship and immigration last summer.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext: No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext: Yes, yes.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext: The Governor General's car was practically outside the door when you brought on your estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
We began our estimates Friday afternoon and completed them Saturday night, or perhaps it was Thursday afternoon and Friday night; I have forgotten which. And, Mr. Speaker, while I do not mean to go far afield in the matter of citizenship and immigration, I should point out that we have just gone through a long debate on the address, and I do not think there has been any reference of any significance to that department in any of the speeches made by my hon. friends opposite. However, it is the desire

it is my desire, and one can understand why it should be-that that department should go before the estimates committee for consideration, so we shall not have any further reference to my having left that department to the last two days of the last session for consideration.
I always like to listen to the hon. member for Prince Albert, and long ago I made up my mind I would not intervene when he was out of order because eventually he does come back to the point. He did speak at some length about the Auditor General and his comments in the public accounts report about some of our past activities. He made a great point of the fact that the C.B.C. had, as he said, defied the Auditor General in connection with a certain bookkeeping method. Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not know what defiance is in his parlance, but the fact of the matter is that the Auditor General did make comments. It is true that those comments were not acted upon immediately, but I for one would expect that I should have time to consider a report of the Auditor General and devise something within the complaint he makes and within the administrative problems that I have to face. As the hon. member finally admitted, the wrong that he claims was done has now been rectified, and we need not be concerned about that in the future.
He also pointed out, and I think in a manner that would leave the impression that something wrong was being done, that the

Auditor General had made certain other observations about practices in the C.B.C. and other crown companies. The very recitation of those things is an indication that no information has been withheld from the opposition. I have been astonished to find almost every speaker in the opposition suggesting that the purpose of the estimates committee which we are recommending to the house is a somewhat devious one on my part to bring about an easier passing of the estimates for which I am responsible.
I cannot imagine any sensible person believing them when they say that. I should have thought that if they complained that the present practice has worked to their disadvantage, the government, if it wanted it that way, would continue the present practice. On the other hand, as I said in my opening statement no government should ask parliament to pass almost $5 billion without the most careful scrutiny, consideration and intelligent criticism which can be given to it. In my capacity as Minister of Finance I think everyone will appreciate that if they could find a way of reducing the estimates,
I would be particularly happy.
On that point, I notice the hon. member for Quebec South is not with us at the moment.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext: Yes, he is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext: I beg your pardon. He was modest enough not to make any reference to his past, and of course I should not either; but I would like to point out that hon. members have not followed his practice very much in recent years, perhaps for reasons of their own. Some years ago the hon. member for Quebec South had occasion to move in the house that an item of the estimates be reduced. My recollection is that he carried that against the government of the day. That was the kind of activity which he considered at that time a private member ought to undertake in order to save the minister of finance something for his next budget.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext: Will the minister permit a question? Does the minister recall an occasion some five years ago when I did the same thing in connection with an item in the estimates of the Minister of Transport, and the Minister of Transport said it was a vote of non-confidence in the government? The whip was cracked and all hon. members opposite came in and voted down the reduction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
The house knows perfectly well my views about party activity in this house. It is the duty of the government to carry on the business of the country. It is the duty of the opposition to do their best to indicate the weaknesses in the policies being
Special Committee on Estimates followed by the government; and if in accordance with that duty they can make motions in this house which would topple the government, then I think it is their duty to take that step.
On the other hand, my hon. friend asked me whether I am aware of what he tried to do. I confess I am. I recall the occasion, and certainly I would not suggest that he should not follow that course. If he tries to do it on my own estimates I shall try to defeat him, but I would be the first to admit his right to take the action he has indicated.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext: Would the government regard it as a vote of non-confidence? There is not much chance of saving money if the government takes that attitude.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL SELECT COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER CERTAIN ESTIMATES
speechtext:
I think I have answered all the direct questions. However, I should comment on what has been said by the hon. member for Kamloops. It will be noted that his opinion about the nature of this committee differs radically from that of others in his own party. He thinks in terms of a committee-and I understand the hon. member for Greenwood shares this view-economy-minded in the sense of trying to cut down the estimates by showing that all the money is not needed. On the other hand, I take it that other members of his party think not so much in terms of an economy measure as of an exploratory measure which would arm them with better information to debate policy. I am not going to say which of the two will result, because I am quite sure the committee will find by experience what is the best course to follow.
The point I am making is this. I am glad we circumscribed the activities of the committee in the first instance, so that it would know what to do. If hon. members choose to work in the committee, as I think they will, with the objectives in view that have been discussed today, they will find, after some time, what are the limits and what are the advantages of the committee, and they will be able to report to the house on details of the estimates in such a manner that the two main results I have mentioned will probably occur.
I would point out that at no time did I place the saving of time first. I said that the committee would give members, both on the committee and off the committee, more information so there would be more intelligent discussion in the committee of supply. When the estimates come back from the estimates committee it may well be that we shall not have the detailed cross-examination about a particular item, but that we shall have a longer policy debate than has been the case up to the present time. Most members of
976	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry the opposition have expressed the desire that that should be so; that we should not waste the time of the committee of the whole on details.
I leave it to the committee, Mr. Speaker, to work it out. I think we should give them all the encouragement we can, and I hope that after not necessarily one year, but perhaps two or three years, we shall find that this committee is in fact functioning to the advantage of the taxpayers of Canada, both with respect to economy and greater criticism of policy which will be possible in the committee of supply.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for York West (Mr. Hamilton) asked this question:
Is the minister aware that Queen Charlotte Airlines of Vancouver has received an offer or offers of purchase substantially in excess of the asset value of the company, and is it the government's intention to attempt to recover part or all of the quarter of a million dollar subsidy paid to the said company in the last two years if the sale transaction is consummated?
I am informed that only after the interests concerned have reached agreement are

International Rivers
arrangements for sale or purchase of airline companies submitted to the air transport board for approval. In the case of Queen Charlotte Airlines, no such agreement has been submitted and therefore I am not able to comment on the matter.
As far as the second part of the hon. member's question is concerned, the financial assistance granted to Queen Charlotte Airlines earlier was a subsidy and not a loan.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, February 4, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe (Port Arthur) for the second reading of Bill No. 3, respecting the construction, operation and maintenance of international river improvements.

maintopic: INTERNATIONAL RIVERS
subtopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in continuing this debate I wish to refer for a moment to a speech made in this house by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) and some of the statements contained therein. I have since had an opportunity to read this speech, and I have found in his remarks things I did not expect to find from a speaker from the socialist ranks. However, in a report of a meeting which he attended in the city of Revelstoke on the night of January 5 I found a very good
indication of what might be the socialist stand, and I would like to quote from the report of that speech:
The Kaiser dam would yield the B.C. government a million dollars a year for 50 years, plus some percentage of power developed. The C.C.F. party objected to the Kaiser company having this right, because it was a private company.
That is the kind of statement I expect to hear from a socialist, and I respect any socialist who stands up for his convictions and expresses what he actually believes. But I was certainly disappointed when the hon. member made no reference whatsoever in this house to this attitude and, in fact, I have come to the conclusion that he made a statement here that might well have come from the other side of the house. However, there is one statement he made in Revelstoke with which I am in full agreement. The report reads as follows:
"What is needed," Mr. Herridge said, "is a meeting of minds of the federal and provincial governments on this matter."
I agree with that 100 per cent, Mr. Speaker.
I now turn to the main features of this bill and some of the political aspects attributed to it in the press throughout the country. I have here a clipping from the Vancouver Province carrying the headline "Ottawa Will Stop It". Then follows the subheading "B.C.'s Kaiser Dam Project 'CockEyed', says Howe". The report goes on to say:
Trade minister C. D. Howe described the agreement between the B.C. government and the Kaiser interests in the United States for a storage dam without on-site power on the Arrow lakes as "a cock-eyed and improvement deal."
I do not like that word "improvement", and I believe possibly they mean "improvident"; but I am not going to correct the press, though it does not sound right. Nevertheless I cannot help but like that word "cockeyed". It shows that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) is quite a human fellow after all, and that off the record and possibly on the spur of the moment he made this very human statement. However, I cannot agree with the thoughts behind that statement.
A little further on, discussing development projects in Canada with a newspaper man, he made it plain that this was one project which would not be realized in its present form if the federal government had anything to do with it. He also made it plain that Ottawa had a lot to do with it, and was confident that legislation now being drafted would block the Kaiser dam plan. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is definite proof of the claim I made that this bill is nothing more or less than a political measure.

International Rivers
I am also going to put on record a couple of cases which I think are similar, and in which the action was not questioned, or disallowed. In fact there seemed to be no reason why any action should have been taken by the federal government toward the British Columbia government of that day. When the West Kootenay Power and Light Company made application for additional storage of water at Kootenay lake, a part of the Columbia river system, the international joint commission agreed that this was desirable in order to firm up power downstream. In this case "downstream", of course, is in Idaho in the United States of America. In this instance the federal government, knowing full well that the province of British Columbia would get no financial return for the extra storage, -and I would ask hon. members to remember that; no financial return-endorsed the plan.
